title: Four Divisive 2016 Movies That Deserve Another Look Ten Years Later
excerpt:
The Neon Demon, Yoga Hosers, Knight of Cups and Swiss Army Man were hardly universal critical favorites.
A decade later, their unusual artistic choices make them fascinating films to revisit.
body_md:
A decade after their release, some of 2016's most divisive films look considerably more interesting than their initial critical reception might suggest. Not every poorly reviewed movie is a hidden masterpiece, but certain productions reward viewers who approach their unusual choices on their own terms.

Nicolas Winding Refn's The Neon Demon is a striking example. Elle Fanning plays an aspiring model drawn into a beautiful but predatory Los Angeles fashion world. The film's deliberately artificial dialogue, glossy compositions and Cliff Martinez score were dismissed by some reviewers as empty style. Yet those qualities can also be read as part of its critique of an industry obsessed with surfaces. Cinematographer Natasha Braier's carefully composed images are central to that interpretation.

Kevin Smith's Yoga Hosers offers a very different case for reconsideration. Starring Lily-Rose Depp and Harley Quinn Smith as teenagers battling bizarre miniature villains, the horror-comedy remains messy and intentionally ridiculous. Its appeal is less about conventional filmmaking polish than the chemistry of its leads and its gleefully eccentric B-movie sensibility. Johnny Depp, Justin Long and Austin Butler also appear.

Terrence Malick's Knight of Cups, starring Christian Bale, was criticized for its drifting narrative and philosophical self-absorption. With Emmanuel Lubezki behind the camera, however, its impressionistic journey through Hollywood and modern alienation can be compelling for audiences comfortable with Malick's poetic approach. Cate Blanchett and Natalie Portman are among the supporting cast.

Perhaps the most revealing reassessment belongs to Swiss Army Man, the feature debut of directors Daniel Kwan and Daniel Scheinert. Paul Dano plays an isolated man who befriends a corpse portrayed by Daniel Radcliffe. What initially looked like an elaborate joke about bodily functions develops into a strange, compassionate exploration of shame, loneliness and the pressure to perform socially acceptable identities. The directors later won major recognition for Everything Everywhere All at Once.

These are critical reevaluations, not claims that contemporary reviews were objectively wrong. Together, the four films show how adventurous storytelling can become easier to appreciate after its initial shock has faded.
seo_title: Four Misunderstood Movies From 2016 Worth Revisiting
seo_description: Revisit The Neon Demon, Yoga Hosers, Knight of Cups and Swiss Army Man, four divisive 2016 films with lasting creative appeal.
